canberra.title: We won’t ever again see a movie like The Odyssey
canberra.snippet: Homer’s The Odyssey has long been considered one of the greatest pieces of fiction ever written. It has been adapted hundreds, if n...
canberra.content:
Christopher Nolan and Matt Damon unite for their third film together in The Odyssey. Photo: Universal Studios.

Homer’s The Odyssey has long been considered one of the greatest pieces of fiction ever written.

It has been adapted hundreds, if not thousands, of times in its nearly 3000-year history. Odysseus’ journey back from the Battle of Troy to the Kingdom of Ithaca is as legendary as it gets.

So, how does a story that has been read by millions find a way to become relevant once again in a time of the internet and spoiler culture?

The answer? Give the story to one of the best directors to ever pick up a camera, give him a blank cheque and let him go to work.

Christopher Nolan is that director and his adaptation of The Odyssey is so grand, so epic and so brilliant, we may never see a movie like it again.

If for some reason or another you don’t know, The Odyssey follows the king of Ithaca, Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his decades-long journey home after the end of the Trojan War.

While away, his wife and Queen consort, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), rules the kingdom while new suitors, including Antinous (Robert Pattinson), all compete for her hand in marriage.

Meanwhile, Odysseus’ son Telemachus (Tom Holland) travels the Greek Isles, looking for any sign that his father survived the voyage home.

The Odyssey is the definition of the word epic. It features swords and sandals, navigating the high seas, mythological monsters, witches, Greek gods and even a massive wooden horse.

A movie of this scale is hard to review without scatter-gunning points left, right and centre, so instead let’s break it down piece by piece.

The first is the IMAX presentation. The Odyssey is the first film shot completely in IMAX 70 mm, making it the most difficult film ever to see properly. What this means is, unlike digital cameras, which are shot on the wide-lens aspect ratio of 2.39:1, IMAX 70 mm uses more vertical space with a 1.43:1, effectively meaning there is more captured in camera with a clearer image.

These cameras are extremely rare and expensive and there are only 41 screens in the world that can properly show the film. Australia’s only one is in Melbourne.

Regardless of whether you see it in 70 mm or not, it means that the movie looks crystal clear and grand in scale regardless of the cinema you see it in. Already, the movie looks and feels as epic as the subject matter it’s tackling.

Next is the actual production. The costumes and sets here are incredible. For context, Nolan claims that there were no computer-generated images in this film, only enhancements to existing places, props or puppets.

This makes every location feel real and lived in, every sword feel battle-tested, every ship like it’s just been sailed and every costume like it has a story of its own. It’s truly awe-inspiring.

Now let’s move on to the narrative. This film isn’t linear and it doesn’t adapt everything from Homer’s narrative, but the way it’s structured is fantastic.

It throws you in the deep end immediately, putting the viewers in the difficult situation that both Penelope and Telemachus find themselves in. Odysseus has been gone for 20 years and for the first half hour, Nolan intentionally doesn’t show his face.

When we eventually do see him, he’s weathered, scarred and almost a shell of a man. It’s then that we are taken back 20 years, to when Odysseus is pulled into the Trojan War.

As it recounts his journey from Troy to the beach he is stranded on, we slowly uncover just how difficult his journey home was and the sins he committed that have left him jaded.

We slowly peel back the psyche of Odysseus by travelling back and seeing the iconic events like the Trojan Horse, the Cyclops and the Island of the Giants, all while cutting back to Penelope and Telemachus’ battle to fight off the suitors.

That brings me to the cast. This thing is packed! Damon gives his best performance in years; meanwhile, Holland gives the best performance of his career.

Anne Hathaway will be in contention for the Best Supporting Actress Oscar come March next year, while John Leguizamo as Eumaeus and Samantha Morton as the witch, Circe, in the best sequence of the entire film, will no doubt get some buzz as well.

Pattinson turns in a great performance as a punchable antagonist; meanwhile, Hamish Patel, Charlize Theron, Jon Bernthal, Lupita Nyong’o and Elliot Page, who could all star in their own films respectively, round out a crazy good cast.

Finally, I’ll touch on the music.

It’s a lock that Ludwig Göransson will nab his fourth Oscar for Best Original Score. The soundtrack is equal parts haunting, inspiring, devastating and mysterious. The fact that he recreated instruments that have been forgotten by history to create the music for this production is absolutely insane and creates sounds probably never heard by anyone alive before.

I could say the film being three hours is a bit long or that I would have liked more context about Odysseus’ motivations to actually go to war, but the fact is this: I don’t actually care because this movie has stuck with me for over a week.

I’ve seen it twice in cinemas, once in IMAX and once in Xtreme Screen and quite frankly, I’ll probably go again before its cinematic run is done because it is a masterpiece.

The Odyssey is now showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: Living safely, worrying constantly: How immigration rhetoric is affecting Indian students
canberra.snippet: Every few weeks, the phone rings. “Are you safe?” It’s the question Indian students in Canberra say they hear most ofte...
canberra.content:
The March for Australia rallies in August 2025 were widely condemned as racist. Photo: Facebook.

Every few weeks, the phone rings. “Are you safe?”

It’s the question Indian students in Canberra say they hear most often from parents back home.

The calls usually come after another news report about Australia’s immigration debate, another political speech blaming migrants for housing shortages or the rising cost of living, or another social media video showing anti-immigration protests.

Thousands of kilometres away, families watch from India and worry. For the students living through it, the reality is often far more complicated.

None of the students Region spoke to could describe being attacked because they were Indian. None could recall an incident of outright racial abuse. Yet almost all admitted they carry a lingering fear that wasn’t there when they first arrived.

“I can’t point to a single incident that has happened to me,” Raj (name changed), a University of Canberra student, said.

“I don’t know if I’ve really experienced racism. But yes, I constantly live with this fear.”

That feeling resurfaced earlier this month when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Australia.

Outside his hotel, right-wing activist Hugo Lennon and other protesters gathered carrying Australian flags and anti-immigration placards, including signs reading “Modi Go Home and take the rest with you”. Police maintained a strong presence while members of the Indian community attended events linked to the visit.

For many Australians, it was another political protest. For students watching from university campuses, it was another reminder that migrants have increasingly become part of Australia’s political conversation.

“I think the news affects our families much more than us,” another postgraduate student from India said.

“They call after watching something online and ask if we’re okay. Then we start questioning ourselves too.”

She admits every unsuccessful job application occasionally sends her mind down an uncomfortable path.

“I always try to tell myself it’s probably not because I’m Indian. But those thoughts do come.”

The students say the anxiety is difficult to explain because it rarely comes from something they have personally experienced. Instead, it builds slowly through headlines, political rhetoric and conversations on social media. Only once did Nisha (name changed) genuinely feel afraid.

She was walking to work when she unexpectedly came across an anti-immigration protest. Nobody approached her. Nobody threatened her.

The demonstration remained peaceful. Yet she still remembers wanting to disappear. “I was petrified,” she said.

“I just wanted to hide somewhere. I wanted to make sure nobody noticed me.”

Months later, she still remembers that feeling, not because anything happened, but because she feared something might.

The students say life as an international student was already becoming more difficult before politics entered the conversation.

The Australian dollar continues to stretch family finances, while the Indian rupee has weakened, making tuition fees and everyday expenses increasingly difficult to manage.

The Federal Government has also increased the base international student visa application fee to $2500 and capped new international student commencements at 295,000 for both 2026 and 2027.

“Eating out is never really an option,” Raj said. “We simply can’t afford it.”

Viswa (name changed), an Australian National University student, said financial pressure often leaves international students vulnerable in the workplace.

“I’ve never been paid weekend penalty rates,” he said.

“Despite Australia’s minimum wage, many international students end up accepting around $17 an hour because they don’t think they have another choice.”

For him, the economic pressures and political debate often feed into each other. “When migrants keep getting blamed for everything, people back home naturally worry about us.”

A common thread ran through Region‘s conversations with students. While many spoke of growing anxiety, none had personally experienced the incidents they feared.

None of those interviewed could describe even a mild racist attack. None knew close friends who had been assaulted because they were Indian.

Most said Australians they met through university, work and their neighbourhoods had been welcoming. The fear, they said, had largely been built through perception rather than personal experience.

“I tell my family back home not to read the news,” Viswa said with a laugh. “That’s probably the best way to feel safe.”

Despite the anxiety, none of the students said they regretted choosing Australia. Most still hope to build careers here, apply for permanent residency and eventually raise families.

For Nisha, the contradiction is impossible to ignore. “I honestly don’t know what the truth is anymore,” she said.

“But as a young woman, I actually feel completely safe when I walk home alone.”

For these students, the headlines and their everyday lives often tell two different stories. The politics may sometimes leave them questioning whether they belong.

But it is the people they meet, in classrooms, workplaces and neighbourhoods, that keep convincing them they do.

canberra.title: Canberrans aren’t just surviving winter anymore – we’re celebrating it
canberra.snippet: Cold enough for you? Right, now we’ve gotten that traditional greeting out of the way – let’s move beyond our thinly veiled winter ...
canberra.content:
Has Canberra stopped gritting its teeth through winter and started embracing a new identity around it? Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Cold enough for you?

Right, now we’ve gotten that traditional greeting out of the way – let’s move beyond our thinly veiled winter whinges and look at the reality of this time of year in Canberra.

First of all, it’s a delight.

Sun-drenched bluebird days keep us active in the great outdoors and topped up with vitamin D, while crisp nights encourage us to don our coziest clothing and cluster festively around crackling firepits, shoving anything warm down our throats and making no apologies for it.

But it hasn’t always felt this magical.

As a born-and-bred Canberran, long have I partaken in the annual hibernation of our people.

Some time after Anzac Day, around the time we permit ourselves indoor heating, residents of capital country bid each other farewell in a joking-not-joking acknowledgement that the antisocial season is upon us and we’ll see everyone again in spring.

More accurately, we’ll pop out again briefly for ‘fake spring’ – those tricky two weeks when Canberra lures us out of hiding before insta-freezing us again as a hilarious seasonal prank.

But this year is different.

Repeatedly, I’ve found myself voluntarily leaving the safe embrace of my ugg boots and Oodie in pursuit of more cultured winter experiences.

And I’m sensing a change in the air which has nothing to do with the barometer.

Firepits are popping up unexpectedly like toadstools. Marshmallows and hot chocolates have become a staple for any outing. And I’ve never seen so many trees wearing knitwear.

It’s all kind of … chic.

Okay, chic might be pushing it, but Canberra winter is definitely distinguishing itself as a vibe.

It’s alpine. It’s trendy. It’s wholesome. It’s faux-European, without trying too hard.

It’s frosty bushwalks admiring iced-over puddles and glistening spider webs. It’s finding a favourite fireplace to warm up with a local wine. It’s baskets of blankets and overhead heating at every cafe. It’s thawing your hands with – obviously – bloody good coffee.

Some of this is naturally occurring, organic phenomena bred from having a highly educated, highly professional, high-income capital city in the frosty foothills of a sub-alpine rural region.

But what’s really special is seeing business and the ACT Government lean in to the Canberra cold, capitalising on our region’s unique qualities to boost business, build community and attract tourism.

Rather than isolating this winter, I’ve been coaxed out of hiding – like a moth to a flame – to businesses and events which celebrate the season. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

From Winter in the City at City Walk to Winter in the Woods at the Arboretum, my family has been lured from our living room with promises of fire twirling and circus acts, lantern-making and star-gazing.

As I run errands, I note that businesses are increasingly adapting amenities and making thoughtful design choices which keep shoppers comfortable for longer in chilly conditions – fireplaces and firepits, radiant heaters, enclosed terrace dining structures.

And it feels like Canberra’s entrepreneurial spirit is giving rise to quirky new experiences almost daily.

Wanna build a snowman? It’s an hour’s drive for toboggans and snowball fights at Corin Forest. Truffle hunting is an incredibly niche activity it feels like every Canberran has experience in. And a winter’s walk around Lake Burley Griffin – once a tragically under-utilised centrepiece of our city – now features climate-controlled domes for snowglobe-inspired dining and floating wood-fired saunas for sweating out that more-ish mulled wine.

Cool enough for you yet?

All this cozy evidence points me to a heart-warming conclusion: winter in Canberra is no longer a time to retreat, but to gather.

Cold snaps are no longer something we complain about or avoid, but leverage and celebrate.

One scarf-wearing tree at a time.

canberra.title: Keep an eye out for Wood Ducks waddling across roads with offspring in tow
canberra.snippet: One of Canberra’s common natural night sounds is one we often hear, though perhaps without putting a name to it. On a quiet night, especi...
canberra.content:
A Wood Duck pair, male on the left with dark brown head, female with more extensive underside patterning. Photo: Ian Fraser.

One of Canberra’s common natural night sounds is one we often hear, though perhaps without putting a name to it. On a quiet night, especially if you live near a grassy oval or park, you may hear a chorus of strong nasal honking “ngaow” passing overhead.

This is a flock of Wood Ducks on the way to graze on the grass for the night. I’m sure you’ve seen them by day, as they are the most common and familiar of Canberra’s duck species.

They are a neat upright grey duck with speckled undersides, most often seen loafing during the day in flocks near urban ponds and wetlands, farm dams, lakes and our major rivers, the Murrumbidgee and Molonglo. They’ll take to the water if we approach too closely but otherwise are comfortable ashore.

The males are very distinctive with coffee-brown heads and a little crest (they’re sometimes also called Maned Ducks), while females are paler and their undersides are more heavily splashed with white blotches. Wood Duck beaks are rather “unducky”; narrow and hooked at the end, reflecting their grass-eating lifestyle.

These feeding flocks are very tightly bound together for part of the year and are loyal to their daytime camps. They’ll return nightly to their favourite grass-restaurant until they’ve eaten it down, then they’ll find somewhere else to feed for a while.

However, by now the autumn flocks have broken up as the pairs, which form long-term bonds, scatter to start the breeding process.

They rely on nesting hollows in standing trees (living or dead) and such hollows are a scarce resource as old trees are regularly removed to make way for suburbia – we don’t try very hard to incorporate original trees into our suburbs, even though we know how important they are for wildlife.

To make the hollow-housing situation even worse, many hollows are taken over by introduced and very aggressive mynas and starlings and colonies of feral honeybees.

Female Wood Duck perched on a branch, honking to assert her ownership of the nearby nesting hollow. Photo: Ian Fraser.

Though their feet aren’t really made for perching, pairs of Wood Ducks are right now staking their claims to hollows by standing on a branch near a desirable nesting hole and shouting their whiny honks at others who may be looking too closely at their chosen home.

The eggs are laid directly on the wood at the bottom of the hollow and covered with down to help keep them warm.

The mother broods alone as her mate has gone to seek out the nearest water for when the chicks hatch.

Because the demand for hollows is so high, the most desirable ones near water are soon taken, so some ducklings hatch not only high above the ground but far from water.

This is the most dangerous time of their entire lives, coming as soon as they hatch. Obviously there is no duckling food in the tree and the mother can’t bring food to them – although they’ll be vegetarian for most of their lives, growing chicks need protein so they need to be able to access insects and small water crustaceans almost immediately.

Fortunately they can walk from the moment they hatch, but first they have to get to the ground.

A pair of Wood Ducks with their ducklings. Broods of a dozen are not uncommon, though most won’t make it to adulthood. Photo: Ian Fraser.

It’s a dramatic scene with the parents urgently encouraging them to jump, both by calling from the ground and by flying repeatedly up to the nest. One after another the little balls of fluff float down to the ground, bounce slightly and are ready for the hazardous trek to the nearest water.

If they are threatened the mother will pretend to be injured, dragging a wing on the ground, while the babies hide in the grass.

Nor is the defence only passive – I’ve been angrily threatened by Wood Duck parents for daring to ride past them as they stood by the lake some 10 m away with their brood. Once the threat has passed she will come back and continue to lead them to the pond or dam where they’ll feed until they can fly.

However one threat that she can’t protect them from is traffic. If you see ducks on the road in spring or summer, please don’t assume that they’ll just fly out of your way – there could well be a train of flightless ducklings behind, as we’ve experienced.

Sometimes we can get so familiar with a common animal that we forget how interesting and attractive they are, which is always a pity.

Keep an eye on your local Wood Ducks as they get into the busiest time of their year.

canberra.title: Raise a glass to history at Speaker’s Corner bar
canberra.snippet: Walking into the Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel always feels a little like stepping back in time, where you’re sur...
canberra.content:
Michael Mueller has designed the Speaker’s Corner cocktail list. Photo: Hyatt Hotel Canberra.

Walking into the Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel always feels a little like stepping back in time, where you’re surrounded by warm wooden panelling, chandelier lighting, brass fittings and 20s architecture.

This 102-year-old building has seen more than its fair share of history and the Speaker’s Corner bar is no exception. Tucked between a leafy courtyard and a games room with an historic billiards table, Speaker’s Corner is the place where politicians, spies, diplomats and socialites spilled secrets over cocktails.

A new cocktail menu seeks to celebrate some of the characters who have played a significant role in Canberra’s history. Slipping onto a bar stool on a bitterly cold winter’s evening, I was ready to hear their stories.

Bartender Michael Mueller is the man behind the menu. He told Region he wanted to keep things refined – “definitely not a tikki vibe!” – by adding his twist on classic cocktails.

I started with Gallagher’s Gimlet: honouring, of course, former ACT Chief Minister (now ACT Senator) Katy Gallagher. The base of this drink is a local gin, mixed with snowpea-mint-basil puree, lime, agave and finger lime. It is refreshing, zesty and light, although I would argue much too Green for a Labor politician!

Michael assured us that Senator Gallagher has tasted the drink and approves.

The herbacous Shepherd’s Sour was a surprise winner for me. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

The Shepherd’s Sour is a herbaceous take on a whiskey sour, with a cucumber and lemon myrtle foam topping a combination of two whiskies. I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this drink. Initially I was sceptical about the combination but it was incredibly well balanced: the foam bringing a little sweetness to the smooth whiskey.

This drink celebrates renowned horticulturist Charles Weston, known as the man who planted three million trees. He landscaped early Canberra and was also responsible for choosing the trees at the Hyatt. So it’s only appropriate to name this herbaceous drink for him.

The Isabella Southwell is a sparkling, vintage-inspired drink that pays homage to the first manager of the hotel.

A pioneering woman, Isabella was ahead of her time to hold such a position in 1924. The drink is described as being “effervescent, elegant, and unforgettable – just like the woman who welcomed Australia’s elite with grace and grit”.

We also tasted the Murdoch Old Fashioned. J S Murdoch was the architect of the original Hotel Canberra in 1924. Dark chocolate, orange bitters and Bourbon whiskey combine for a smoky smooth drink.

Murdoch Old Fashioned is surely best enjoyed by a roaring fire. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

One cocktail on the menu hasn’t been altered at all: The Menzies Martini. This is, of course, a nod to Sir Robert Menzies who was Australia’s longest-serving Prime Minister and a frequent guest at the hotel. You can order the Menzies Martini with three oysters on the side, just as he liked to have it.

The atmosphere in the Speakers Corner bar is second to none. The fireplace roars behind us, as lamps and candlelight create intimate corners (perfect for a clandestine meeting).

There’s a compact menu of snacks, sandwiches and sweets on offer. In a charming old-fashioned touch, a small dish of peanuts or olives will accompany your drinks.

Sipping our drinks I couldn’t help but wonder what stories these walls would tell us if they could talk. But perhaps the next best thing is raising a glass to that history.

Speaker’s Corner Bar is at Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel, 120 Commonwealth Avenue. It is open from 4 to 11 pm Monday to Thursday, 3 pm until midnight Friday and Saturday and 5 to 9 pm on Sunday.

australia.title: ‘Socialist’ teachers target eight Victorian Labor MPs including education minister – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed ‘We’re cohesive’: PM says after muted ALP national conference The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , spoke with D...
australia.content:
‘Rebel teacher’ to contest Victorian education minister’s seat in state election

A group of self-described “rebel teachers” in Victoria are running a campaign to target eight sitting Labor MPs, including the minister for education, Ben Carroll, in November’s state election.

The candidates are members of the “Socialists in Schools” group, in opposition to the department of education. Victorian Socialists have announced they are aiming to contest every lower house seat in Victoria.

Brendan Laws is going up against Carroll in his formerly safe seat of Niddrie, calling for the ending of public funding to high-fee private schools, the abolition of Naplan and full funding for uniforms, excursions, materials and lunches.

Laws said the Victorian school system had been underfunded for years.

There’s a consensus that public education deserves better. On the issue of education, the ALP is not just out of touch – they’re on the other side of the picket line, with the Liberals and One Nation.

Economic segregation is increasing, as working-class students are more and isolated while high-fee private schools get more and more funding each year. This must end immediately.

Key events

  • 7h ago

    What we learned: Sunday, 26 July

  • 8h ago

    Fuel excise relief extension unlikely as war threatens price hike

  • 9h ago

    Investigation into police shooting after bystander allegedly hit with stray bullet in Queensland

  • 10h ago

    ‘Rebel teacher’ to contest Victorian education minister’s seat in state election

  • 10h ago

    Australia leads Commonwealth Games medal tally

  • 11h ago

    PM to raise ‘unjustified’ US tariffs with Trump, says fuel excise relief won’t be extended

  • 12h ago

    PM opposes telehealth for euthanasia

  • 12h ago

    Coalition says PM sort to ‘shut down debate’ at Labor's national conference

What we learned: Sunday, 26 July

With that, we will wrap the blog for the afternoon. We’ll be back first thing tomorrow morning but until then, enjoy the rest of your Sundays.

Here’s a recap of the major developments of the day:

  • The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told Insiders the government isn’t planning to extend the fuel excise relief, due to lapse on 2 August, as the war in the Middle East drags on.

  • Albanese also said he was a supporter of voluntary euthanasia but opposed allowing patients to use telehealth to access it, as the Greens and independent Kate Chaney plan to introduce legislation based on changes to Labor’s national platform.

  • Australia is leading the top of the Commonwealth Games table at the pared-back event in Glasgow, with 12 gold and 23 medals overall.

  • An internal police investigation has been launched after a bystander was shot during a tense standoff between officers and an armed offender in Cairns.

  • And a group of self-described “rebel teachers” in Victoria are running a campaign to target eight sitting Labor MPs, including the minister for education, Ben Carroll, in November’s state election.

Ex-commandos behind army chopper crash memorial

The memorial for the four aviators who died in a helicopter crash was spearheaded by Operation Pilgrimage, an organisation of former commandos.

“The actual anniversary is only two days off. I selected this weekend for that very purpose,” the Operation Pilgrimage chair, Allan Miles, told AAP.

“It’s been a real privilege to be involved in the planning and then doing the hard yards to get it up and running.”

“I was quite lifted that there’s a sense of sadness, of course, but also acknowledgment amongst themselves that something has moved forward,” Miles said.

A Defence Flight Safety Bureau report into the Taipan tragedy found the primary cause of the crash was “spatial disorientation”, which happens when a pilot misperceives the position of an aircraft in relation to the environment.

It concluded the pilots were likely experiencing fatigue levels shown to “impede optimal performance” and increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation.

Earlier in July, a Senate inquiry examining the crash was told regulator Comcare had referred two briefs of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions relating to fatigue management and the TopOwl helmet-mounted display system worn by the pilots.

The regulator was informed by federal prosecutors a year earlier they did not intend to prosecute the defence force because they did not consider there were reasonable prospects of obtaining a conviction.

Comcare’s chief executive, Colin Radford, told the inquiry the regulator believed prosecution should proceed.

The inquiry is due to report in September.

Separate probes are being held by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force and the Queensland coroner.

Memorial unveiled for army chopper crash victims

A memorial for aviators who died in an army helicopter crash is being unveiled almost three years on from the tragedy, AAP reports.

Capt Danniel Lyon, Lt Maxwell Nugent, WO Class Two Joseph Laycock and Cpl Alexander Naggs were killed when their MRH-90 Taipan chopper crashed into waters off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands during Exercise Talisman Sabre on 28 July 2023.

Their loved ones joined Queensland’s governor, Jeannette Young, at Airlie Beach’s Shute harbour on Sunday for the official unveiling of a memorial commemorating the men’s lives. The project was spearheaded by Operation Pilgrimage, an organisation of former commandos. Whitsundays regional council supported the initiative and successfully lobbied for a Queensland government grant.

The crew, from the Sydney-based 6th Aviation Regiment, were flying in a helicopter given the call-sign Bushman 83 when it crashed during a training exercise. Nineteen family members of the Bushman 83 crew have flown in from Melbourne, Sydney, Canberra and other parts of the country for the event and gathered for a group dinner on Saturday night.

It is estimated almost 50 Australian Defence Force members have died in training activities in the past 30 years.

Fuel excise relief extension unlikely as war threatens price hike

The US-Israeli war with Iran will probably drive petrol prices above $ 2 a litre in the coming weeks, but the government has no plans to extend its fuel excise relief when it ends in a week.

AAP reports:

Fuel excise relief for motorists is unlikely to be extended despite the war in the Middle East flaring up.

The Labor government halved the fuel excise for three months from April in response to rising prices as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, saving drivers 32 cents a litre on fuel.

The measure was extended for a further month in July, but at a reduced rate of 16 cents per litre.

The extension is due to lapse on 2 August.

Fresh tensions between the US and Iran have caused Brent crude oil prices to rise to more than $US100 a barrel, but Anthony Albanese has indicated continued excise relief is not on the cards.

“That’s not in our planning at this point in time,” the prime minister told ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday.

“(Fuel) usage has come down and is indeed lower than it was a year ago as well, but importantly as well, we have kept supply going.”

Albanese indicated some fuel-related measures were in the pipeline.

“We’ll have some more announcements about fuel in the coming days and weeks as well,” he said.

“We’ll continue to examine things that were in that process in the budget.”

Drivers have been warned petrol prices could reach more than $2 a litre as the excise discount is wound back.

Average prices for unleaded petrol have climbed to more than $1.80 per litre in all state capitals in recent days, up from about $1.50 at the end of June.

The jump in oil prices comes as Iran-aligned Houthi militants fired on Saudi oil installations on the coast of the Red Sea and Tehran attempted to shut down shipments through the strait of Hormuz again.

US strikes have recommenced in response to Iranian attacks on vessels travelling through the strait, a key oil transit route.

Albanese said a continuation of the conflict would lead to economic pressure.

“The war is having an impact here in Australia and the longer it goes, the bigger the impact will be,” he said.

“This is a war on the other side of the world.

“We are not protagonists in it, but we are impacted by it, and we’ve consistently called for a de-escalation.”

‘Awkward’ selection drama won’t derail Aussie sprinters

Rohan Browning has put the Commonwealth Games track selection drama in the rear vision mirror as he seeks to spearhead Australia’s sprint charge in Glasgow.

The 28-year-old former national champion was picked alongside the current title holder, Lachie Kennedy, and Kiwi defector Eddie Nketia in a three-pronged 100m assault.

It begins on Monday at Scotstoun Stadium, with the men’s 100m heats among the first events on the Games athletics program before nine finals are contested in the evening session. Australia’s 100m selection call sparked a challenge from Josh Azzopardi, whose appeal, heard by the National Sports Tribunal, was ultimately unsuccessful.

Azzopardi said he felt “absolutely robbed” by the decision, but hoped it wouldn’t dent the mood in an Australian camp eyeing unprecedented track success at the Games. It appears there are no hard feelings from Browning, who is adamant the saga hasn’t dampened his relationship with Azzopardi.

The pair are both part of Australia’s five-man 4x100m relay squad in Glasgow, and worked together at training camps in Italy and Spain in the lead-up to the Games. “The nature of going through an appeal process can make this feel a little personal, but ultimately it’s not,” Browning told AAP.

-AAP

Tom McIlroy

Labor under pressure to allow telehealth for euthanasia but PM opposed

Labor will come under pressure to implement changes to its national policy platform and allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth services, with the Greens and independent MP Kate Chaney to introduce legislation.

This week’s Labor national conference in Adelaide changed the party’s platform and committed to overturn a Howard-era law banning people from having medical appointments regarding euthanasia via telehealth services.

New language added to the platform suggests Labor MPs would have a conscience vote on the issue, but the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Sunday the government might not progress laws through parliament.

Read the story here:

Rate watchers eye inflation data and RBA chief’s speech

Economists are awaiting key quarterly inflation data but expect the Reserve Bank to hold interest rates despite renewed fighting in the Middle East sending oil prices up again. The Australian Bureau of Statistics will publish the consumer price index’s second quarter on Wednesday, which shows household inflation.

The Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, will also speak in Sydney on Tuesday, with her speech to be closely watched for indicators on how the central bank intends to approach inflation risks.

Taylor Nugent, a NAB senior economist, says the bank does not believe another rate rise is likely in 2026 despite oil prices rising again due to tensions between the US and Iran.

Our position is there will be enough confidence in growth slowing in the labour market so that rates don’t need to be tightened further.

That’s despite risks such as elevated inflation, renewed cost pressures and new oil price levels. The Reserve Bank’s board will next meet in more than two weeks, with the Commonwealth Bank noting the “backdrop shifting rapidly”.

The housing market has deteriorated, household spending is slowing from the elevated pace seen earlier this year and businesses’ capacity to pass on higher costs is likely weaker following three interest rate hikes.

The Reserve Bank was expected to keep rates on hold for the remainder of 2026, the CBA said.

-AAP

Investigation into police shooting after bystander allegedly hit with stray bullet in Queensland

An internal police investigation has been launched after a bystander was allegedly shot during a tense standoff between officers and an armed offender, AAP reports.

The woman was one of two people allegedly shot by police in Cairns, in north Queensland, on Saturday night. Ethical standards are investigating the incident after a woman was allegedly hit by a stray bullet when officers opened fire on an armed offender.

Police had been called to Benjamina Street in the southern Cairns suburb of Mount Sheridan, about 5.10pm on Saturday after reports of a man armed with knives and an attempted armed robbery. They found the 28-year-old man at a roundabout and shot him.

The state’s police minister, Dan Purdie, was reluctant to comment in detail on the shooting as it was under investigation, but said he had seen footage. He told reporters on Sunday:

They are highly trained. They do have equipment, and I’m sure some of those operational matters have probably all been answered by the police this morning. I acknowledge the situations, the dangerous situations, police have put themselves in.

It’s the second high-profile Queensland police shooting in three days. It follows the shooting of a police officer and the death of a man after a domestic dispute at Yengarie, near Maryborough, on the state’s Fraser Coast, on Friday evening.

The ethical standards command is investigating the incident, with oversight from the Crime and Corruption Commission, and it will be reported to the coroner.

Homicide police investigating after woman found dead in Melbourne home

In Victoria, homicide squad detectives are investigating the death of a woman whose body was found at a home in Melbourne yesterday.

In a statement, Victoria police said the 73-year-old woman was found dead inside a Fitzroy North home about 1am.

The cause of death is yet to be determined. An investigation into the suspicious death is ongoing.

Why are Labor women overlooked as Albanese’s potential successor?

On Thursday, Kate Ellis was elevated to become Labor’s national president, leading for the first time an all-female team at the top of the party’s organisational wing, with two female vice-presidents.

The former Rudd and Gillard government minister joins the Australian Council of Trade Unions president, Sally McManus, and its secretary, Michele O’Neill, as some of the most powerful members of the labour movement.

But as the federal caucus, again for the first time, has more women than men, they barely get a mention in discussions about who will succeed Anthony Albanese.

Read the piece from Krishani Dhanji here:

Tom McIlroy

Albanese dodges questions on Point Piper dinner with donors hosted by billionaire’s son

Anthony Albanese has tried to avoid answering questions about a Labor fundraising dinner hosted by the son of a Chinese billionaire under scrutiny from the tax office.

Felix Lee, the son of Chinese billionaire high roller Phillip Dong Fang Lee, hosted the prime minister at a dinner at a Sydney mansion, reportedly attended by the Commonwealth Bank boss, Matt Comyn, the former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews, the former Asic chair James Shipton and former Future Fund boss David Murray.

Asked directly by the ABC’s David Speers if he attended the Point Piper event, Albanese said: “I attend lots of functions.”

The Sydney Morning Herald reported last week that Phillip Lee had been investigated by the ATO over large sums of money coming from China to Australia.

Speers eventually asked the PM: “Why don’t you want to answer that?”

Albanese, talking in Adelaide on Saturday night, replied: “Well, I do, you just said that that occurred. You know, that’s fine. I attend lots of dinners, in lots of places, and I don’t talk about private dinners. I have held a number this week here in Adelaide as well.”

Asked whether it was appropriate for Labor to fundraise from families under scrutiny by authorities, Albanese said he was “not aware of those issues”.

I attend a lot of meetings, functions, with lots of people. I mean, talking about people’s relatives, even removed from that.

australia.title: Albanese at odds with Labor policy which now says telehealth should be allowed for euthanasia consultations
australia.snippet: Campaigners say existing federal ban on phone or video calls for assisted dying consultations adversely affects people living in regional...
australia.content:
Labor will come under pressure to allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth services, with the Greens and independent Kate Chaney to introduce legislation based on changes to Labor’s national platform.

Last week’s national conference in Adelaide changed the ALP platform and committed Labor to overturn a Howard-era law banning people from having medical appointments regarding euthanasia via telehealth services.

New language added to the platform gives Labor MPs a conscience vote on the issue, but the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Sunday the government might not progress laws through parliament.

The party’s platform is a set of policy principles but changes are not always immediately reflected in government legislation.

Albanese said while he supported assisted dying, also known as voluntary euthanasia, he believed the telehealth change risked undermining proper medical safeguards.

“It is important that people have the right to die … with dignity,” he told ABC TV.

“But it’s also important that protections are placed around it. Now, if someone has a heart attack or an acute health condition, they need a doctor. They can’t do that over telehealth.

“I think someone ending their life is just as important. I think it should be face-to-face recognition and face-to-face engagement. My concern is … the potential for misuse but also the potential it has to undermine the system itself.”

Asked if the federal government would move to change the law to reflect the updated national platform, Albanese said the cabinet would decide on whether new legislation would be drafted, in consultation with MPs.

“Governments determine what governments do around our cabinet table. What the conference does is put the general direction of what they want, and it’s clear that it’s a matter of conscience,” he said.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young on Sunday indicated she would quickly move ahead with a private member’s bill on the issue, an apparent attempt to force Labor’s hand.

The Curtin MP, Kate Chaney, had said on Friday that she would move to reintroduce her own private member’s bill in the lower house, saying it would give Labor “the earliest opportunity to bring this cruel anomaly to an end and give country people the same access as Australians in the big cities”.

“This overdue change in Labor policy on voluntary assisted dying should mean an end to the needless suffering of people in the final stages of life, particularly for those in regional areas who are currently forced to travel, sometimes repeatedly, just to access lawful medical care,” she said.

Andrew Denton, a longtime campaigner and the founding director of Go Gentle, said access to care should not depend on someone’s location.

“The PM is a supporter of end-of-life choice and he’s right to ask questions about the safety of using telehealth in the VAD process,” Denton said on Sunday.

“For reassurance, he need look no further than the expert advice from medical groups such as the Australian Medical Association and Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, who say telehealth can and should be a safe adjunct to VAD services, certainly where the patient is too sick to travel or when a doctor cannot reach the patient in time.

“It makes no sense that advice cannot be given by videoconference or scripts sent by email. Palliative care routinely discusses life-and-death decisions via telehealth and describes it as ‘particularly important’ in providing comprehensive supportive care in the last weeks of a patient’s life. There is no good reason to treat VAD any differently.”

Doctors and advocates for voluntary assisted dying have long called for changes, arguing the telehealth ban adversely affects patients who live in rural and remote areas, and those whose conditions limit their movement or make travel painful.

The federal criminal code prohibits the use of a carriage service to incite or encourage suicide, so health professionals risk breaking the law if they use telecommunications for many aspects of the VAD process.

Fines of up to $300,000 are also possible for breaches of the law.

Disparities between state and federal laws currently add to delays to patients obtaining approval for voluntary assisted dying, which is particularly problematic for those with health conditions leading to rapid decline, and who want to die at home.

While state laws differ, generally, patients must make at least three requests for access to voluntary assisted dying to their doctor, and be assessed at least twice by medical professionals. Doctors require these appointments to be in person so that they do not breach federal laws.

Labor’s updated national platform says the party will “remove barriers that exist in federal law to the provision of end-of-life care (including via telehealth) as part of lawful access to voluntary assisted dying in the states and territories, while maintaining appropriate clinical safeguards”.

It also guarantees a conscience vote on the issue, where MPs are not bound by the government’s position on a bil

australia.title: Mega datacentre planned for outer Melbourne will be six times bigger than a large shopping centre
australia.snippet: More than 3,600 people sign petition for careful assessment of proposed AI hub, now a flashpoint for national debate on datacentre boom F...
australia.content:
For some residents it started with a letter in the mailbox. It was a “friendly introduction from the team behind the Victorian AI hub”.

“I am knocking on doors to explain what we have in mind and, most importantly, to listen,” the letter from Syncline Energy stated.

“Construction won’t start for at least two-years while we complete the planning and environmental approvals.”

For others, news of the project had already spread through social media and news reports, which sounded the alarm before the company had begun its communication efforts.

The site for what has been dubbed a mega datacentre in Plumpton, about 30km north-west of the Melbourne CBD, is now an empty paddock next to Melbourne’s renewable energy hub, just off the Calder Freeway. It’s near a fast-growing suburb, transmission lines, and a stone’s throw from where Harry Houdini made what was claimed to be Australia’s first controlled powered flight in 1910. Planes from nearby Tullamarine airport fly low overhead, and on weekends the sky is punctured by the lights and sounds of the Calder speedway.

This paddock is rapidly becoming a microcosm of the growing community resentment to datacentres across Australia.

The proposed site is 350 hectares, of which Syncline says 40% – 140ha, or just under six times the size of Chadstone shopping centre – will be used to house four datacentre buildings with maximum capacity of 2.4GW, with the remaining 60% to be open land. The proposed centre is larger than any currently operating in Australia and would consume more electricity than is generated by Victoria’s largest power station, Loy Yang A.

The sheer scale of the project has alarmed residents before shovels have hit the ground, building on a growing deep discomfort with the explosion in datacentre construction. An April report by lobby group Data Centres Australia said there were 30 datacentres in operation in Victoria, with another 30 in the pipeline.

Environmental impacts, electricity and water use, concerns about the rise of AI more broadly, and the impact of campaigns in the US – which show developments stretching for miles, lit up like an international airport and with a constant hum of white noise and higher power prices – are feeding community concerns.

A petition calling on the state government to “ensure the environmental, cultural, social and infrastructure implications of the proposed Victorian AI Hub are fully assessed and publicly considered,” as well as the cumulative effects of other new datacentres, has amassed over 3,600 signatures. It was started by Molly Walker, who lives over 250km away in the Grampians and first heard about the plans on TikTok.

Walker, who works in conservation, said the scale of the project made her think “enough is enough”.

“How much is being taken away from the environment?” she asked.

“There’s also the noise … I’ve heard a lot about the datacentres in America and how much noise they produce. I did some research and found they’re not much different from the ones here in terms of the impact.”

Other locals feel the western suburbs have become “a dumping ground”.

“They always say they can’t put datacentres out in the east because of the land. The west has these vast lands and because of the socio-demographic areas [of the east] people there are likely to complain,” says Dr Karen Austria.

Austria grew up in the area, and is an electrical engineer by training. She says locals are concerned the industrial development could lead to a drop in house prices.

She also points to the fact the location is within a green wedge, which the state government has said should have its environmental, economic and cultural values protected.

“Why are you putting this in our back yard?” she asks.

“They’re promising to do community consultation … but everyone has got this one letter, and they feel like they don’t know enough about it yet and the company needs to communicate more.”

‘Desirable’ scale

Much of the community anger about the wave of datacentres in development has stemmed from a lack of community consultation, and through fast-track approval processes that skip the lengthy council review to go straight to the state government.

The managing director of Syncline Energy, Phil Galloway, says the company is carefully consulting with locals before submitting the planned application for the Plumpton site.

“The process starts with our direct neighbours and works out from there. The conversations will take at least a year,” he says.

Ecological surveys and cultural heritage work is being undertaken parallel to the community discussions, Galloway says, adding that locals need to be shown there will be no noise, heat island, traffic, ecology issues or pollution, “which means careful engineering, architecture and urban planning”.

“It would be insincere if we submitted a planning permit and then sought that input later,” he says.

Galloway says the large scale of the project is all about building sovereign AI capability, and making efficient use of land, energy and water. The size of the land will allow buffers and green space between the buildings and residents. It’s also almost entirely under the Melbourne airport flight path, which means there are planning restrictions against using it for housing.

The company is promising to use solar, wind and battery storage and provide additional transmission and grid stability. Galloway says it will also create local jobs, a community fund and walking and cycling paths.

“That scale can only be delivered through a major precinct connecting into the main 500kV grid rather than piecemeal smaller datacentres in the suburbs and rural towns,” he says.

“From a network stability point of view, it is desirable to concentrate the datacentre load at a strong point in the grid and install buffering equipment so to stabilise any IT load changes.”

A Facebook group created in opposition to the project has more than 300 members.

The city of Melton is already feeling the heat, and was forced to clarify its role will be limited if the application goes to the state government.

Opposition to the plan has also reached the offices of local federal MPs, with Labor’s Alice Jordan-Baird and Sam Rae releasing a statement earlier this month saying they would write to the Victorian government and Syncline to ask how the project aligns with the federal government expectations on datacentres and AI infrastructure.

“The west cannot simply become the destination for infrastructure that places additional strain on resources while delivering little in return,” the statement read.

Balancing risks

The rapid expansion of datacentres in Australia has experts warnings of a massive impact on the nation’s energy and water supplies.

The NSW Net Zero Commission said this week that the booming number of datacentres “could have ramifications for the electricity sector’s transition”.

A federal parliamentary inquiry into datacentres began in May, and a NSW inquiry is ongoing. There have been calls for a moratorium on new developments until the federal government introduces new rules.

The Australian government’s framework for the energy and water-hungry developments would create a legal obligation for large-scale datacentres to underwrite new power supply, pay their full share of grid connection, and add as much energy to the grid as they take out of it, Albanese said this month.

The new policy will aim to find the balance between growing community concerns, the desire for sovereign AI capability, and the potential for billions in investment – and still get buy in from the states to properly plan for the growth of the sector.

The Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, told the state parliament in May that Melbourne was the “key destination for datacentre investment”.

The Victorian minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, later told an economic forum that it was not a question of how many datacentres the state can build but “what kind of Victoria we build around them”.

australia.title: SA premier Peter Malinauskas at the ALP national conference - podcast

australia.content:
Speaking with political editor Tom McIlroy and chief political correspondent Dan Jervis-Bardy at the 50th Labor conference in Adelaide, Peter Malinauskas talks about his own state contest with One Nation and why progressives should not speak down to Pauline Hanson’s supporters.

And despite the US admitting this week that the production rate of Virginia-class submarines has not increased, the SA premier argues that abandoning Aukus would pose an even greater risk than the controversial agreement’s potential problems

australia.title: Connected under the Milky Way: new exhibition shares Indigenous astronomical knowledge from Australia to South Africa
australia.snippet: The Yamaji-Wajarri people studied the wide-open skies of their country for millennia before being host to one of the world’s largest radi...
australia.content:
Carlleen Dingo’s earliest memories are of looking up at the inky black skies above Australia’s north-west coastline, awash with planets, stars and galaxies. Geraldton, or Jambinu, is a coastal town 400 kilometres north of Perth, known for its wildflowers, red earth, fierce winds and undulating sandy dunes.

But at night, there’s another world on display.

The Yamaji-Wajarri people have looked to the skies for thousands of years as a teacher and a guide.

“At night-time, living out in the bush, [I] always sat around the fire and looked up, looking at the embers flicking in the air. There’s a sky full of stars.

“You get curious and you watch, and then you watch them move. And when you move to different places on country, you try and look for them stars and pin them down.”

Growing up, Dingo heard the stories from her grandmothers about how her ancestors would travel and hunt by reading the skies.

“Pops used to point out: ‘Oh, that star there, that’s the Milky Way’… you understand how the travellers travelled back in the day by using the stars and going through country at night.”

That relationship is explored in a global exhibition showcasing how Indigenous artists from Australia and South Africa see the night sky. The exhibition, called Cosmic Echoes: A shared sky has toured Africa and Europe before coming back to Australia.

Dingo is one of the artists involved. She says the scale of the exhibition began to sink in when she followed her paintings journey from her Geraldton home across the Indian Ocean. “I got told that my painting was going to go on a tour going to Africa,” she says. “Then it went to Manchester and Luxembourg in Europe and I was like: ‘Well, all right then!’”

Linked by the stars

About 300 kilometres inland from Geraldton, the arid red earth is punctured by native grasses, spinifex, and saltbush, and bursting wildflowers that spring up after the rains. This isolated and sparsely populated region is home to one of the largest satellites and radio telescopes in the world.

Dr Douglas Bock, director of the CSIRO’s space and astronomy unit, says the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, or Murchison radio-astronomy observatory, on Wajarri country is the result of a decades long relationship between the agency and the Wajarri Yamaji Aboriginal Corporation.

“We’ve been working now in this area, I think, for around 20 years,” he says. “That was when we first started looking at this place and seeing the Murchison region as one of the best places in the world to do astronomy.”

It hosts the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) observatory’s SKA-Low telescope. An array of 131,072 two-metre tall antennas resembling metal Christmas trees, spread across 74 kilometres, working as one telescope. The technology maps distant galaxies, cosmic magnetic fields and black holes.

Prof Jessica Dempsey has also looked up at the skies for as long as she can remember. The radio astronomer and director-general of the SKA observatory says the exhibition is an artistic exploration of science, technology and astronomy spanning two continents.

“We can only learn more by sharing the stories and the ways of looking at the world across these different communities,” Dempsey says.

The SKA observatory is also building a mid-frequency telescope in South Africa’s arid Karoo region, the SKA-Mid telescope, comprising of 196 dish antennas, each standing almost 15 metres tall.

For South African artist Junior Oliphant, a First Nations person who grew up in a coloured town still grappling with the brutal and racist impacts of colonial rule and apartheid, identity is complex.

“In South Africa, we take pride in the word ‘coloured’, but for me it’s also complicated,” Oliphant says. “I’d like to believe that my ancestry is Khoisan, but it isn’t something I can just claim. I don’t have the elders’ guidance or mentorship to find out who I am or where I’m coming from. So the question of ‘who am I, where do I come from’ is a question I’m asking through my paintings.”

His painting in the exhibition depicts Dr Katrina Esau, or Ouma Katrina, a traditional language speaker and fierce advocate. He was then able to meet her at the Cape Town opening of the exhibition.

“Ouma Katrina is the last living N|uu speaker in the world. She’s like the last living link between a lost culture and a lost language,” he says.

Oliphant has now travelled to Geraldton for the Australian opening of the exhibition, and speaks about the ways Indigenous cultures in the southern hemisphere are connected through time and space by stories about the Milky Way. In Khoisan folklore, he says, “there was this girl who was kept in a cage, and she cried out until the cage exploded. The ashes flew into the sky and that is how the Milky Way was created.”

“The Khoisan in South Africa used the stars like compasses – to guide when to move, when new plants would come, when seasons changed,” Oliphant says. “With the Wajarri people, there are similarities in what they see in the stars too. Even though we are worlds apart, I feel like two different Aboriginal groups are connected under one star light.”

Dempsey says it took western technology centuries to catch up to the astronomical knowledge held by First Peoples. She gives the example of the Seven Sisters, also known as the Pleiades star cluster, which are found grouped together in the stories of many different cultures.

“One of the pieces of astronomy that all of our Indigenous family knew a long time ago is, how did they know they were sisters? All of these stories of these particular stars are a family, and so already in the story, they’e depicted by a lot of artists … as a family,” she says.

“It took us another several thousands of years before we had the technology to confirm that in a western science way.”

For Dingo, there is a deep sense of pride in knowing her people are recognised as the rightful hosts of some of the world’s most ambitious science and technology.

“As a little Yamatji running around that bush, I never ever thought that this would be available,” she says. “We’ve got the biggest satellites sitting out on country. That’s something to be proud of, because you always want to be the biggest and the best.”

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.
